questions.question: Why is calling `fs.readFileSync` inside an HTTP request handler a problem, while calling it once at startup is acceptable?
options: readFileSync is deprecated and will be removed
It blocks the single event loop thread, so every other request waits while the disk is read
It always returns a Buffer, which cannot be sent in a response
It reads the file on the libuv thread pool and therefore loses errors
questions.explanation: Synchronous fs calls block the event loop. At startup nothing else is waiting, but inside a handler they stall all concurrent requests.

questions.question: Your code checks `fs.existsSync(file)` and then calls `readFile(file)`. What is the better pattern?
options: Call existsSync twice to be sure
Just attempt the read and handle an error with code ENOENT, avoiding the race between the check and the read
questions.explanation: Check-then-act is a race: the file can change between the two calls. Attempting the operation and branching on err.code is both simpler and correct.

questions.question: Which approach gives an atomic file update so a crash never leaves a half-written file?
options: Write to a temp file in the same directory, then rename it over the target
Write to a temp file in the OS temp directory, then copy it over the target
questions.explanation: rename is atomic within one filesystem, so readers see either the old or the new file. A temp file elsewhere may be on another filesystem, and copying is not atomic.

questions.question: What does `await mkdir("a/b/c", { recursive: true })` do if the directories already exist?
options: Throws an error with code EEXIST
Throws an error with code ENOENT
Succeeds without an error, like mkdir -p
questions.explanation: With recursive: true, mkdir creates any missing parents and does not fail when the path already exists.
